5	A reusable passive cold-chain carrier has an insulated outer shell, a removable product tray, a removable thermal module, and an insulated lid. The tray side walls are spaced inward from the shell side walls to form two side supply passages.

It includes a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings aligned with the side supply passages. Warm air rising from the product region enters the central inlet, divides along faces of the cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage. The carrier is passive. It has no fan, pump, or powered air mover.
8	
9	The lid carries a depending indexing rib. As the lid closes, the rib enters a mating channel in the spacer frame and shifts the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages. A compressible lid gasket seals against the upper edge of the shell after registration. The same closing movement presses resilient feet of the spacer frame against ledges of the shell so that the module cannot lift away from the tray during transport.
10	
11	A removable absorbent wick lies in a shallow condensate channel around the product tray. Openings at the lower ends of the guide ducts discharge condensate into the channel. A pull tab on the wick remains accessible when the product tray is removed, allowing the wick to be replaced without opening a phase-change cassette.
12	
13	The shell includes a mechanical exposure indicator visible from outside. An indicator stem is thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette and retained by a temperature-responsive latch. If that cassette softens enough to release the latch, a spring moves the indicator stem to a latched exposed position. The indication remains exposed after the cassette cools again and is reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The indicator does not control airflow.
14	
15	For use, conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame, products are placed in the tray, the thermal module is placed above the tray, and the lid is closed to register and retain the module. The disclosed essential relationship is the registered passive circulation path around the removable tray and opposed cassettes, combined with lid-driven registration of the thermal module. The wick and the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator are supported optional features.

file.content: The present disclosure relates to reusable insulated carriers for temperature-controlled distribution of payloads, and more particularly to a passive carrier in which a removable thermal module holding phase-change cassettes is registered by closing an insulated lid so that a circulation path is established around a removable product tray without any powered air mover.

content.content:
1	Temperature-sensitive payloads such as medicines, diagnostic samples, and perishable foods are frequently distributed in insulated containers that carry their own thermal reserve. A container of this kind is loaded at a packing point, handed to one or more carriers, and opened at a destination that may be many hours away. Because the container travels unattended and often without electrical power, the thermal behaviour of the container has to be set at the moment of closing and cannot be corrected in transit.
2	
3	Two practical difficulties dominate the use of such containers. The first is the distribution of cold within the payload space. A thermal reserve placed against one wall, or laid directly on top of a payload, cools the material nearest to it strongly and the material farthest from it weakly, so the payload experiences a spread of temperatures. Direct contact between the thermal reserve and the payload can drive the contacted items below the intended range while more distant items drift above it. Moving air distributes the effect of the reserve more evenly, but a fan, pump, or other powered air mover adds a battery, a failure mode, and a service burden, and is unwelcome in a container that has to be washed, stacked, and returned.
4	
5	The second difficulty is that a container which relies on an internal air path only performs as intended if that path is actually present when the container is closed. Loose internal components are lifted, rotated, or nudged during loading and during transport. If the passages that are supposed to carry conditioned air downward are displaced relative to the passages that are supposed to carry it back, the intended path is broken and the container behaves as an ordinary insulated box, without any outward sign that anything is wrong. Placing that responsibility on the person who packs the container is unreliable, because a component that is merely set in place looks the same whether or not it is correctly positioned.
6	
7	Related handling problems arise in reusable service. Condensate forms on cold surfaces inside a closed container and collects where it is difficult to reach. Removing it commonly means handling the thermal reserve itself, which is undesirable when the reserve is a sealed phase-change cassette that should not be opened in the field. Finally, a payload that has been briefly warmed can arrive at a temperature that appears correct, so a recipient inspecting the container at delivery cannot tell from the contents alone whether the thermal reserve lost its condition earlier in the journey.
8	
9	There remains a need for a reusable passive carrier in which the internal circulation path is established positively by the act of closing the container, in which the thermal reserve is held in that established relationship during transport, and in which routine servicing and evidence of thermal exposure are available without opening the thermal reserve.
10

Temperature-sensitive payloads such as medicines, diagnostic samples, and perishable foods are frequently distributed in insulated containers that carry their own thermal reserve. A container of this kind is loaded at a packing point, handed to one or more carriers, and opened at a destination that may be many hours away. Because the container travels unattended and often without electrical power, the thermal behaviour of the container has to be set at the moment of closing and cannot be corrected in transit.

Two practical difficulties dominate the use of such containers. The first is the distribution of cold within the payload space. A thermal reserve placed against one wall, or laid directly on top of a payload, cools the material nearest to it strongly and the material farthest from it weakly, so the payload experiences a spread of temperatures. Direct contact between the thermal reserve and the payload can drive the contacted items below the intended range while more distant items drift above it. Moving air distributes the effect of the reserve more evenly, but a fan, pump, or other powered air mover adds a battery, a failure mode, and a service burden, and is unwelcome in a container that has to be washed, stacked, and returned.

The second difficulty is that a container which relies on an internal air path only performs as intended if that path is actually present when the container is closed. Loose internal components are lifted, rotated, or nudged during loading and during transport. If the passages that are supposed to carry conditioned air downward are displaced relative to the passages that are supposed to carry it back, the intended path is broken and the container behaves as an ordinary insulated box, without any outward sign that anything is wrong. Placing that responsibility on the person who packs the container is unreliable, because a component that is merely set in place looks the same whether or not it is correctly positioned.

Related handling problems arise in reusable service. Condensate forms on cold surfaces inside a closed container and collects where it is difficult to reach. Removing it commonly means handling the thermal reserve itself, which is undesirable when the reserve is a sealed phase-change cassette that should not be opened in the field. Finally, a payload that has been briefly warmed can arrive at a temperature that appears correct, so a recipient inspecting the container at delivery cannot tell from the contents alone whether the thermal reserve lost its condition earlier in the journey.

There remains a need for a reusable passive carrier in which the internal circulation path is established positively by the act of closing the container, in which the thermal reserve is held in that established relationship during transport, and in which routine servicing and evidence of thermal exposure are available without opening the thermal reserve.

A reusable passive cold-chain carrier is disclosed. The carrier includes an insulated outer shell, a removable product tray, a removable thermal module, and an insulated lid.

The removable product tray is suspended above a shell floor by tray feet so that a lower return passage remains under the removable product tray. Tray side walls of the removable product tray are spaced inward from shell side walls of the insulated outer shell to form two side supply passages. The removable product tray has perforations.

The removable thermal module includes a rigid spacer frame holding two opposed phase-change cassettes. The rigid spacer frame rests above the removable product tray and below the insulated lid. The rigid spacer frame includes a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings aligned with the side supply passages.

The carrier is passive and has no fan, pump, or powered air mover. Warm air rising from a product region enters the central inlet opening, divides along faces of the phase-change cassettes, descends through the downward guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through the perforations in the removable product tray, and returns through the lower return passage. The circulation path therefore surrounds the payload rather than acting on it from one side, and it is driven by the density difference that the phase-change cassettes themselves create.

The insulated lid carries a depending indexing rib. As the insulated lid closes, the depending indexing rib enters a mating channel in the rigid spacer frame and shifts the removable thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages. The act of closing the carrier therefore establishes the circulation path, instead of relying on the person who packs the carrier to place the removable thermal module accurately. A compressible lid gasket seals against an upper edge of the insulated outer shell after registration, so the removable thermal module is aligned before the interior is closed off. The same closing movement presses resilient feet of the rigid spacer frame against ledges of the insulated outer shell so that the removable thermal module cannot lift away from the removable product tray during transport.

In some embodiments, a removable absorbent wick lies in a shallow condensate channel around the removable product tray, and condensate discharge openings at lower ends of the downward guide ducts discharge condensate into the shallow condensate channel. A pull tab on the removable absorbent wick remains accessible when the removable product tray is removed, allowing the removable absorbent wick to be replaced without opening a phase-change cassette.

In some embodiments, the insulated outer shell includes a mechanical exposure indicator visible from outside. An indicator stem is thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette and retained by a temperature-responsive latch. 1	In the following description, the terms upper, lower, above, below, inward, and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright attitude of use, in which the insulated lid is uppermost. The described embodiments illustrate the invention and do not limit it. FIG. 1 through FIG. 5 show one carrier, each view showing the parts that view is concerned with, and a part introduced in one view is referred to elsewhere in this description whether or not it is shown in every view.
2	
3	## Overview of the carrier
4	
5	Referring to FIG. 1 and FIG. 2, a reusable passive cold-chain carrier includes an insulated outer shell 10, a removable product tray 20, a removable thermal module 40, and an insulated lid 60. The insulated outer shell 10 has a shell floor 12, shell side walls 14 rising from the shell floor 12, and an upper edge 16 at the top of the shell side walls 14. The insulated outer shell 10, the insulated lid 60, and the walls that bound the interior are of insulating construction, for example a rigid foam core within a washable outer skin, so that the carrier can be cleaned, stacked, and returned for reuse.
6	
7	Referring also to FIG. 4, the removable product tray 20 receives the payload. The removable product tray 20 has a bottom, tray side walls 24, and tray feet 22 depending from the bottom. The tray feet 22 stand on the shell floor 12 and suspend the removable product tray 20 above the shell floor 12, so that a lower return passage 28 remains under the removable product tray 20. The tray feet 22 are spaced apart from one another so that the lower return passage 28 is continuous beneath the removable product tray 20 from one side of the insulated outer shell 10 to the other. The tray side walls 24 are spaced inward from the shell side walls 14 to form two side supply passages 30, each side supply passage 30 extending upward from the lower return passage 28 alongside the removable product tray 20. The removable product tray 20 has perforations 26 through its bottom, distributed across the bottom, so that the interior of the removable product tray 20 communicates with the lower return passage 28.
8	
9	The removable product tray 20 lifts out of the insulated outer shell 10 as a unit, with the payload in it, once the removable thermal module 40 has been taken out. Loading and unloading therefore do not disturb the passages, because the passages are formed by the position that the removable product tray 20 takes up when it is returned to the insulated outer shell 10 and not by any separate ducting that has to be assembled.
10	
11	## The removable thermal module
12	
13	Referring to FIG. 1, FIG. 3, and FIG. 4, the removable thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 holding two opposed phase-change cassettes 44. The rigid spacer frame 42 is a self-supporting frame body, for example of moulded polymer, stiff enough that the phase-change cassettes 44 it carries do not close the passages formed in it. The rigid spacer frame 42 rests above the removable product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60, so that the removable thermal module 40 is lifted out as one piece and the two phase-change cassettes 44 travel with it.
14	
15	The rigid spacer frame 42 includes a central inlet opening 46 through its upper region, two downward guide ducts 48 beside the phase-change cassettes 44, and peripheral outlet openings 50. Each phase-change cassette 44 is a sealed cassette of phase-change material that is conditioned before use, and the two phase-change cassettes 44 are held on opposite sides of the central inlet opening 46 with their faces mutually opposed. Each downward guide duct 48 extends downward beside one of the phase-change cassettes 44 and opens at its lower end. The peripheral outlet openings 50 lie at the periphery of the rigid spacer frame 42 and are aligned with the side supply passages 30 when the removable thermal module 40 is in a registered position.
16	
17	Because the two phase-change cassettes 44 are opposed and are held apart by the rigid spacer frame 42, the air that enters between them is exposed to two cooled faces at once, and no face of the payload is in contact with a phase-change cassette 44. The payload is conditioned by the air that has passed the phase-change cassettes 44, rather than by conduction into a cassette lying on top of it.
18	
19	## The registered passive circulation path
20	
21	The carrier is passive. It has no fan, pump, or powered air mover. Circulation is produced by the density difference between the air warmed by the payload and the air cooled at the faces of the phase-change cassettes 44, and the geometry of the carrier gives that difference a single closed path to follow.
22	
23	In use, warm air rising from a product region within the removable product tray 20 enters the central inlet opening 46, divides along faces of the phase-change cassettes 44, descends through the downward guide ducts 48, enters the side supply passages 30, passes through the perforations 26 in the removable product tray 20, and returns through the lower return passage 28 to the product region. The path is closed on itself and surrounds the removable product tray 20 on the sides and underneath, so that cooled air is delivered to the payload from below and around it and warmed air is drawn off from above it.
24	
25	The path exists only when the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30. If the removable thermal module 40 is set down out of position, the peripheral outlet openings 50 discharge against the tray side walls 24 or against the shell side walls 14, the descending limb of the path is blocked, and the carrier behaves as a plain insulated box. This is the failure that the registration described below is directed to, and it is a failure that gives no outward sign, because a removable thermal module 40 that is merely set in place looks the same whether or not it is correctly positioned.
26	
27	## Lid-driven registration and retention
28	
29	Referring to FIG. 1, FIG. 3, and FIG. 4, the insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62, and the rigid spacer frame 42 has a mating channel 52 that receives the depending indexing rib 62. As the insulated lid 60 closes, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 52 and shifts the removable thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30. The registration is therefore performed by the act of closing the carrier. The person who packs the carrier is not required to align the removable thermal module 40, and cannot leave it misaligned, because the insulated lid 60 does not come down onto the upper edge 16 without carrying the removable thermal module 40 into position.
30	
31	The depending indexing rib 62 and the mating channel 52 are shaped so that the rib meets the channel over a range of initial positions of the removable thermal module 40 and draws it inward as the insulated lid 60 descends, the last part of the closing movement bringing the removable thermal module 40 fully into the registered position. In some embodiments the depending indexing rib 62 and the mating channel 52 are elongate and asymmetrically placed on the rigid spacer frame 42, so that the removable thermal module 40 can be seated in only one orientation and the peripheral outlet openings 50 cannot be presented to the wrong side of the interior.
32	
33	A compressible lid gasket 64 on the insulated lid 60 seals against the upper edge 16 of the insulated outer shell 10 after registration. The order of these two events matters. The depending indexing rib 62 engages the mating channel 52 and completes the registration while the compressible lid gasket 64 is still clear of the upper edge 16, so that the removable thermal module 40 is free to be shifted by the depending indexing rib 62 and is not being asked to move after the interior has been closed off. Only then does continued closing compress the compressible lid gasket 64 against the upper edge 16 and seal the interior.
34	
35	The same closing movement presses resilient feet 54 of the rigid spacer frame 42 against ledges 18 of the insulated outer shell 10, so that the removable thermal module 40 cannot lift away from the removable product tray 20 during transport. The ledges 18 project inward from the shell side walls 14 at the level at which the removable thermal module 40 is seated. The resilient feet 54 are compliant limbs of the rigid spacer frame 42, and the closing insulated lid 60 deflects them against the ledges 18 so that they remain loaded while the carrier is closed. The load holds the removable thermal module 40 down against handling, tilting, and vibration in transit, which would otherwise let the removable thermal module 40 rise and break the overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 50 and the side supply passages 30. When the insulated lid 60 is opened, the resilient feet 54 relax and the removable thermal module 40 lifts out by hand without a tool.
36	
37	Registration and retention are thus produced by the same movement that a user has to make in any event. Nothing has to be latched, clamped, or checked separately, and there is no state in which the carrier is closed and sealed but the circulation path is not established.
38	
39	## Condensate handling and the removable wick
40	
41	Referring to FIG. 2 and FIG. 4, a shallow condensate channel 70 extends around the removable product tray 20, and a removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the shallow condensate channel 70. Condensate discharge openings 56 at lower ends of the downward guide ducts 48 discharge condensate into the shallow condensate channel 70. Moisture that condenses on the cooled surfaces within the downward guide ducts 48 runs down the ducts and leaves them through the condensate discharge openings 56, rather than collecting on the payload or standing in the bottom of the interior.
42	
43	The removable absorbent wick 72 has a pull tab 74. The pull tab 74 remains accessible when the removable product tray 20 is removed, so that the removable absorbent wick 72 is drawn out of the shallow condensate channel 70 and replaced without opening a phase-change cassette 44 and without dismantling the removable thermal module 40. Routine servicing between journeys therefore does not require handling of the sealed phase-change cassettes 44, which are conditioned items that should be returned to conditioning intact. In some embodiments the removable absorbent wick 72 is a strip of absorbent material sized to the length of the shallow condensate channel 70, and the pull tab 74 is an extension of that strip at one end that stands above the rim of the shallow condensate channel 70.
44	
45	## Mechanical exposure indicator
46	
47	Referring to FIG. 1 and FIG. 5, the insulated outer shell 10 includes a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside. An indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette 44 and is retained by a temperature-responsive latch 84. A spring 86 acts on the indicator stem 82 in the outward direction and is held by the temperature-responsive latch 84 while the phase-change cassette 44 remains in condition.
48	
49	If that phase-change cassette 44 softens enough to release the temperature-responsive latch 84, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to a latched exposed position. The indication remains exposed after the phase-change cassette 44 cools again, and is reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The value of this behaviour is that a payload which was warmed part way through a journey and then cooled again arrives at a temperature that looks correct, and the contents alone give the recipient no way to know what happened. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 records the event in the structure of the carrier and holds the record until a person opens the carrier and deliberately resets it.
50	
51	The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. The interior of the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is separate from the circulation path, and the circulation path is the same whether the indicator stem 82 is retained or has moved to the latched exposed position. The thermal condition being reported is taken directly from a phase-change cassette 44, that is, from the reserve that actually conditions the payload, and no electrical power, battery, or logging device is required for the indication.
52	
53	## Method of passively conditioning a payload
54	
55	In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes 44 are fitted to the rigid spacer frame 42 to form the removable thermal module 40, products are placed in the removable product tray 20, the removable product tray 20 is placed in the insulated outer shell 10 on its tray feet 22, the removable thermal module 40 is placed above the removable product tray 20, and the insulated lid 60 is closed. Closing the insulated lid 60 brings the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 52, shifts the removable thermal module 40 into the registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30, presses the resilient feet 54 against the ledges 18, and then compresses the compressible lid gasket 64 against the upper edge 16. Air then circulates passively along the path described above for the duration of the journey.
56	
57	At the destination the insulated lid 60 is opened, the removable thermal module 40 is lifted out, and the removable product tray 20 is lifted out with the payload in it. Between journeys the removable absorbent wick 72 is withdrawn from the shallow condensate channel 70 by the pull tab 74 and replaced, the interior is cleaned, the phase-change cassettes 44 are returned for conditioning, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset by hand if it has moved to the latched exposed position.
58	
59	## Variations
60	
61	The number of perforations 26 and their distribution across the bottom of the removable product tray 20 are chosen for the payload being carried, a wider distribution giving a more even delivery from the side supply passages 30 into the interior of the removable product tray 20. The removable product tray 20 may be provided in more than one depth for the same insulated outer shell 10, the tray feet 22 in each case suspending the removable product tray 20 above the shell floor 12 so that the lower return passage 28 remains. The phase-change cassettes 44 may be exchanged for cassettes of a different phase-change material to suit a different transport range, without any change to the rigid spacer frame 42, the depending indexing rib 62, or the mating channel 52, because registration is a matter of the frame geometry and not of the cassettes.
62	
63	The removable absorbent wick 72 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features. A carrier may be built with the registered passive circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with either optional feature separately, or with both. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another where the combination is physically consistent.
64

The rigid spacer frame 42 is a self-supporting frame body, for example of moulded polymer, stiff enough that the phase-change cassettes 44 it carries do not close the passages formed in it. The rigid spacer frame 42 rests above the removable product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60, so that the removable thermal module 40 is lifted out as one piece and the two phase-change cassettes 44 travel with it.

Referring to FIG. 1, FIG. 3, and FIG. 4, the insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62, and the rigid spacer frame 42 has a mating channel 52 that receives the depending indexing rib 62. As the insulated lid 60 closes, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 52 and shifts the removable thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30. The registration is therefore performed by the act of closing the carrier. The person who packs the carrier is not required to align the removable thermal module 40, and cannot leave it misaligned, because the insulated lid 60 does not come down onto the upper edge 16 without carrying the removable thermal module 40 into position.

The depending indexing rib 62 and the mating channel 52 are shaped so that the rib meets the channel over a range of initial positions of the removable thermal module 40 and draws it inward as the insulated lid 60 descends, the last part of the closing movement bringing the removable thermal module 40 fully into the registered position. Referring to FIG. 2 and FIG. 4, a shallow condensate channel 70 extends around the removable product tray 20, and a removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the shallow condensate channel 70. Condensate discharge openings 56 at lower ends of the downward guide ducts 48 discharge condensate into the shallow condensate channel 70. Moisture that condenses on the cooled surfaces within the downward guide ducts 48 runs down the ducts and leaves them through the condensate discharge openings 56, rather than collecting on the payload or standing in the bottom of the interior.

The pull tab 74 remains accessible when the removable product tray 20 is removed, so that the removable absorbent wick 72 is drawn out of the shallow condensate channel 70 and replaced without opening a phase-change cassette 44 and without dismantling the removable thermal module 40. Referring to FIG. 1 and FIG. 5, the insulated outer shell 10 includes a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside. An indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette 44 and is retained by a temperature-responsive latch 84. If that phase-change cassette 44 softens enough to release the temperature-responsive latch 84, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to a latched exposed position. 1. A passive cold-chain carrier, comprising:

an insulated outer shell having a shell floor, shell side walls rising from the shell floor, and an upper edge at a top of the shell side walls;

a removable product tray within the insulated outer shell, the removable product tray having a bottom with perforations through the bottom, tray side walls, and tray feet suspending the removable product tray above the shell floor so that a lower return passage remains under the removable product tray, the tray side walls being spaced inward from the shell side walls to form two side supply passages, each side supply passage extending upward from the lower return passage alongside the removable product tray;

a removable thermal module comprising a rigid spacer frame holding two opposed phase-change cassettes, the rigid spacer frame resting above the removable product tray and including a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings; and

an insulated lid above the removable thermal module and carrying a depending indexing rib, the rigid spacer frame having a mating channel that receives the depending indexing rib as the insulated lid closes, whereby the depending indexing rib shifts the removable thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages;

wherein the carrier has no fan, pump, or powered air mover, and wherein, in the registered position, the central inlet opening, faces of the phase-change cassettes, the downward guide ducts, the peripheral outlet openings, the side supply passages, the perforations, and the lower return passage define a circulation path that is closed on itself and along which air rising from a product region within the removable product tray returns to the product region.

2. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, further comprising a compressible lid gasket that seals against the upper edge of the insulated outer shell after registration, the depending indexing rib engaging the mating channel while the compressible lid gasket is clear of the upper edge, and continued closing of the insulated lid thereafter compressing the compressible lid gasket against the upper edge.

3. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the rigid spacer frame has resilient feet and the insulated outer shell has ledges, and closing of the insulated lid presses the resilient feet against the ledges so that the removable thermal module cannot lift away from the removable product tray during transport.

4. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 3, wherein the ledges project inward from the shell side walls at a level at which the removable thermal module is seated, and the resilient feet are compliant limbs of the rigid spacer frame that remain loaded against the ledges while the carrier is closed and relax when the insulated lid is opened.

5. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the depending indexing rib and the mating channel are elongate and asymmetrically placed on the rigid spacer frame, so that the removable thermal module is seated in only one orientation.

6. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the two phase-change cassettes are held on opposite sides of the central inlet opening with faces of the phase-change cassettes mutually opposed, and each downward guide duct extends downward beside one of the phase-change cassettes and opens at a lower end of that downward guide duct.

7. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the tray feet are spaced apart from one another so that the lower return passage is continuous beneath the removable product tray from one side of the insulated outer shell to the other, and the perforations are distributed across the bottom of the removable product tray.

8. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the removable thermal module lifts out of the insulated outer shell as one piece with both phase-change cassettes, and the removable product tray thereafter lifts out of the insulated outer shell with a payload in it.

9. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, further comprising a shallow condensate channel extending around the removable product tray, wherein condensate discharge openings at lower ends of the downward guide ducts discharge condensate into the shallow condensate channel.

10. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 9, further comprising a removable absorbent wick lying in the shallow condensate channel.

11. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 10, wherein the removable absorbent wick has a pull tab that remains accessible when the removable product tray is removed, so that the removable absorbent wick is replaced without opening a phase-change cassette.

12. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the insulated outer shell includes a mechanical exposure indicator visible from outside, the mechanical exposure indicator comprising an indicator stem thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette, a temperature-responsive latch retaining the indicator stem, and a spring that moves the indicator stem to a latched exposed position when that phase-change cassette softens enough to release the temperature-responsive latch.

13. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 12, wherein the indicator stem remains in the latched exposed position after that phase-change cassette cools again, and is reset manually only after the carrier is opened.

14. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 12, wherein the mechanical exposure indicator does not control airflow, an interior of the mechanical exposure indicator being separate from the circulation path and the circulation path being the same whether the indicator stem is retained by the temperature-responsive latch or has moved to the latched exposed position.

15. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the phase-change cassettes are exchangeable for cassettes of a different phase-change material without change to the rigid spacer frame, the depending indexing rib, or the mating channel.

16. A method of passively conditioning a payload, comprising:

fitting two conditioned phase-change cassettes to a rigid spacer frame to form a removable thermal module, the rigid spacer frame including a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings;

placing products in a removable product tray;

placing the removable product tray in an insulated outer shell on tray feet that suspend the removable product tray above a shell floor of the insulated outer shell so that a lower return passage remains under the removable product tray, tray side walls of the removable product tray being spaced inward from shell side walls of the insulated outer shell to form two side supply passages;

placing the removable thermal module above the removable product tray;

closing an insulated lid onto the insulated outer shell so that a depending indexing rib carried by the insulated lid enters a mating channel of the rigid spacer frame and shifts the removable thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages; and

thereafter circulating air passively, without a fan, pump, or powered air mover, from a product region within the removable product tray into the central inlet opening, along faces of the phase-change cassettes, downward through the downward guide ducts, through the peripheral outlet openings into the side supply passages, through perforations in the removable product tray, and back to the product region through the lower return passage.

17. The method of claim 16, wherein closing the insulated lid registers the removable thermal module before a compressible lid gasket carried by the insulated lid seals against an upper edge of the insulated outer shell, and continued closing thereafter compresses the compressible lid gasket against the upper edge.

18. The method of claim 16, wherein closing the insulated lid presses resilient feet of the rigid spacer frame against ledges of the insulated outer shell so that the removable thermal module cannot lift away from the removable product tray during transport.

19. The method of claim 16, further comprising, at a destination, opening the insulated lid, lifting the removable thermal module out of the insulated outer shell as one piece with both phase-change cassettes, and thereafter lifting the removable product tray out of the insulated outer shell with the payload in it.

20. A method of servicing a passive cold-chain carrier between uses, comprising:

opening an insulated lid of the carrier and withdrawing a depending indexing rib carried by the insulated lid from a mating channel of a rigid spacer frame of a removable thermal module, the rigid spacer frame holding two opposed phase-change cassettes and having two downward guide ducts beside the phase-change cassettes;

lifting the removable thermal module out of an insulated outer shell of the carrier;

lifting a removable product tray out of the insulated outer shell, thereby exposing a pull tab of a removable absorbent wick lying in a shallow condensate channel that extends around the removable product tray and that receives condensate from condensate discharge openings at lower ends of the downward guide ducts;

withdrawing the removable absorbent wick from the shallow condensate channel by the pull tab and placing a replacement absorbent wick in the shallow condensate channel, without opening a phase-change cassette; and

returning the removable product tray and the removable thermal module to the insulated outer shell and closing the insulated lid so that the depending indexing rib enters the mating channel and shifts the removable thermal module into a registered position in which peripheral outlet openings of the rigid spacer frame overlap side supply passages formed between tray side walls of the removable product tray and shell side walls of the insulated outer shell.

21. The method of claim 20, further comprising resetting by hand a mechanical exposure indicator of the insulated outer shell from a latched exposed position to which a spring moved an indicator stem of the mechanical exposure indicator when a phase-change cassette thermally coupled to the indicator stem softened enough to release a temperature-responsive latch.

1	A reusable passive cold-chain carrier has an insulated shell, a removable product tray, a removable thermal module, and an insulated lid. Tray feet leave a return passage beneath the tray, whose side walls are spaced inward from the shell side walls to form two side supply passages. The module is a rigid spacer frame holding two opposed phase-change cassettes and having a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts, and peripheral outlet openings. As the lid closes, a depending indexing rib enters a mating channel in the frame and shifts the module into a registered position in which the outlet openings overlap the side supply passages. Air circulates without a powered air mover, rising from the product region into the inlet opening, descending the guide ducts into the side supply passages, and returning through tray perforations and the return passage.

input.command: grep -oE '\b(1[0-9]|[2-9][0-9])\b' draft/08-detailed-description.md | sort -n -u | tr '\n' ' '; echo; find . -name 'rendered*' -o -name '*.png' -o -name '*figure-audit*' | tr '\n' ' '
input.description: List numerals used and check for rendered images

content.text: I have read every file in the workspace. Here is what I found.

input.summary: The draft is a faithful, well-organised rendering of the inventor's disclosure at the level of the core invention (shell/tray/module/lid, the registered passive circulation loop, lid-driven registration and retention, the wick, and the irreversible exposure indicator), and the abstract now sits at 140 words, clearing the previous filing gate. Three classes of defect remain. First, no drawing sheets exist at all: figures/ contains five Markdown briefs and no rendered-*.png, and there is no review/figure-audit-evidence.json, so all five described figures and all thirty specification numerals are unillustrated — this is the root cause of both mechanical failures. Second, several structural, material, dimensional and variant details in the description, figure briefs and claims are not traceable to input/disclosure.md or input/conversation.md (the disclosure and the conversation are word-for-word identical, so there is no second source): notably the perforations being "through its bottom", the elongate/asymmetric keying of rib and channel in claim 5, the interchangeable-cassette variant of claim 15 and the multi-depth tray, the foam-core/moulded-polymer materials, the wick's strip geometry, and the ledge/foot specifics in claim 4. Third, the added "bottom" perforation limitation creates a self-contradiction in the recited flow path, which is stated in both directions within a single paragraph and again in claims 1 and 16. No [REF:...] citations appear in the draft and prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is nothing to check under citation fidelity; as the drafting brief notes, no prior-art search was run and the available art is empty rather than merely incomplete.

findings.title: No drawing sheets exist for FIG. 1 through FIG. 5; every specification numeral is unillustrated
findings.detail: The specification describes five figures and uses thirty reference numerals, but figures/ contains only the five Markdown briefs (fig-01.md through fig-05.md) — there is no rendered-*.png for any figure, and review/figure-audit-evidence.json does not exist. A directory listing and a recursive search for *.png / rendered* return nothing. This is the single cause of both mechanical failures reported (five described figures with no sheet, thirty numerals absent from every drawing). It cannot be verified whether the visible geometry and printed numerals agree with the briefs, because no pixels exist to open. Note that the briefs themselves do distribute all thirty numerals across the five sheets (10,16,20,40,60,64,80 / 12,14,20,26,28,30,40,60 / 18,42,44,46,48,52,54,62 / 22,24,48,50,56,70,72,74 / 10,44,80,82,84,86 = 30 distinct), so the drawing plan is complete and only the rendering step is missing.
findings.evidence: draft/07-drawings.md: "FIG. 1 is an exploded perspective view of a reusable passive cold-chain carrier, showing the insulated outer shell, the removable product tray, the removable thermal module, and the insulated lid." — figures/fig-01.md ends "## Reference numerals appearing on this sheet\n10, 16, 20, 40, 60, 64, 80", but `ls figures/` returns only fig-01.md, fig-02.md, fig-03.md, fig-04.md, fig-05.md.
findings.fix: Render one sheet per existing brief (figures/rendered-fig-01.png … rendered-fig-05.png) from the five briefs as written, which already carry every numeral, and regenerate review/figure-audit-evidence.json against the resulting image hashes. No text, numeral definition, or part need be removed or added to satisfy the check.

findings.title: Perforations located "through its bottom" and "distributed across the bottom" are not in the disclosure
findings.where: draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶7 and ¶61; draft/09-claims.md claim 1 and claim 7; figures/fig-01.md, figures/fig-02.md
findings.detail: The inventor says only that air "passes through perforations in the product tray" and never says where those perforations are. The candidate adds a specific location and distribution, carries it into claim 1 as a positive structural limitation of the tray and into claim 7 as a further limitation, and builds figure geometry on it. Location of an opening is a structure, and the candidate's own detailed description cannot supply support it introduced itself. The added location is also what produces the flow-path contradiction reported separately.
findings.evidence: disclosure.md: "enters the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage" — candidate ¶7: "The removable product tray 20 has perforations 26 through its bottom, distributed across the bottom, so that the interior of the removable product tray 20 communicates with the lower return passage 28."; claim 1: "the removable product tray having a bottom with perforations through the bottom"; claim 7: "the perforations are distributed across the bottom of the removable product tray"; figures/fig-02.md: "Perforation 26: small gaps through the thickness of the bottom panel of the tray 20, distributed across that panel".
findings.fix: Recite the perforations only as the inventor did. In ¶7 replace with "The removable product tray 20 has perforations 26 through the removable product tray 20." and delete "so that the interior of the removable product tray 20 communicates with the lower return passage 28."; in claim 1 replace "a bottom with perforations through the bottom" with "perforations through the removable product tray"; delete "and the perforations are distributed across the bottom of the removable product tray" from claim 7; in ¶61 delete the first sentence about the number and distribution of perforations; in fig-02.md change to "Perforation 26: small gaps through the wall of the tray 20 opening into the adjacent side supply passage 30" and in fig-01.md replace "a field of small round through holes distributed across the panel" with a corresponding wall depiction.

findings.title: The circulation path is recited in two mutually exclusive directions in the same paragraph
findings.where: draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶23 (also ¶7, ¶61); draft/09-claims.md claim 1 wherein-clause and claim 16 final step
findings.detail: With the perforations placed only through the tray bottom, air arriving in a side supply passage cannot reach those perforations before reaching the lower return passage: the return passage lies between them. The first sentence of ¶23 orders the path "side supply passages → perforations → lower return passage", while the very next sentence orders it "lower return passage → up through the bottom → payload" by stating that cooled air is delivered from below. ¶7 states the bottom perforations connect the tray interior to the return passage, which is the second order, and ¶61 states delivery runs "from the side supply passages 30 into the interior" through those same bottom holes, which is the first. Claims 1 and 16 both freeze the first order into the claim language. As written, no single geometry satisfies every statement.
findings.evidence: ¶23: "enters the side supply passages 30, passes through the perforations 26 in the removable product tray 20, and returns through the lower return passage 28 to the product region. The path is closed on itself and surrounds the removable product tray 20 on the sides and underneath, so that cooled air is delivered to the payload from below and around it"; claim 16: "through the peripheral outlet openings into the side supply passages, through perforations in the removable product tray, and back to the product region through the lower return passage".
findings.fix: Apply the same correction as for the bottom-perforation limitation: with the perforations no longer confined to the tray bottom, the disclosed order (side supply passages → perforations → lower return passage) is self-consistent throughout. In ¶23 delete "so that cooled air is delivered to the payload from below and around it and warmed air is drawn off from above it", or restate it neutrally as "so that cooled air reaches the payload around and beneath the removable product tray 20". Leave the claim 1 and claim 16 sequences as they stand, since they already track the disclosure's wording.

findings.title: Claim 5 and ¶31 add an undisclosed keying geometry for the indexing rib and mating channel
findings.detail: The disclosure states only that the rib enters a mating channel and shifts the module into the registered position. It says nothing about the rib and channel being elongate, about asymmetric placement on the frame, about a resulting single permitted orientation, about the rib meeting the channel over a range of initial positions, or about the rib drawing the module inward during descent. These are added shape, placement and function assertions, and one of them is claimed.
findings.evidence: disclosure.md: "As the lid closes, the rib enters a mating channel in the spacer frame and shifts the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages." — ¶31: "The depending indexing rib 62 and the mating channel 52 are shaped so that the rib meets the channel over a range of initial positions of the removable thermal module 40 and draws it inward as the insulated lid 60 descends... In some embodiments the depending indexing rib 62 and the mating channel 52 are elongate and asymmetrically placed on the rigid spacer frame 42, so that the removable thermal module 40 can be seated in only one orientation and the peripheral outlet openings 50 cannot be presented to the wrong side of the interior."; claim 5: "wherein the depending indexing rib and the mating channel are elongate and asymmetrically placed on the rigid spacer frame, so that the removable thermal module is seated in only one orientation."
findings.fix: Delete ¶31 in its entirety and cancel claim 5, renumbering claims 6–21 and their dependencies accordingly. The disclosed registration function is already stated in ¶29 in the inventor's own terms and claimed in claim 1.

findings.title: Claim 15 and the Variations paragraph add undisclosed variants (interchangeable cassette chemistries, multiple tray depths)
findings.detail: Neither the disclosure nor the conversation mentions cassettes of a different phase-change material, a different transport range, interchangeability without change to the frame, rib or channel, or a tray offered in more than one depth. These are added variants presented as part of the invention, and one of them is a claim limitation.
findings.evidence: ¶61: "The removable product tray 20 may be provided in more than one depth for the same insulated outer shell 10... The phase-change cassettes 44 may be exchanged for cassettes of a different phase-change material to suit a different transport range, without any change to the rigid spacer frame 42, the depending indexing rib 62, or the mating channel 52"; claim 15: "wherein the phase-change cassettes are exchangeable for cassettes of a different phase-change material without change to the rigid spacer frame, the depending indexing rib, or the mating channel." The disclosure says only "conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame" and "a rigid spacer frame holding two opposed phase-change cassettes".
findings.fix: Delete the second and third sentences of ¶61 and cancel claim 15, renumbering the remaining claims. Retain the last paragraph of ¶63, which restates the inventor's own statement that the wick and the indicator are supported optional features.

findings.title: Undisclosed materials of construction asserted for the shell, lid and spacer frame
findings.detail: The disclosure identifies the shell and lid only as "insulated" and the frame only as "rigid", and says the carrier is reusable. It names no material. "Rigid foam core within a washable outer skin" and "moulded polymer" are specific material constructions introduced by the candidate; common engineering knowledge and plausibility are not source support.
findings.evidence: ¶5: "The insulated outer shell 10, the insulated lid 60, and the walls that bound the interior are of insulating construction, for example a rigid foam core within a washable outer skin, so that the carrier can be cleaned, stacked, and returned for reuse."; ¶13: "The rigid spacer frame 42 is a self-supporting frame body, for example of moulded polymer, stiff enough that the phase-change cassettes 44 it carries do not close the passages formed in it." Disclosure: "A reusable passive cold-chain carrier has an insulated outer shell... and an insulated lid"; "The thermal module is a rigid spacer frame holding two opposed phase-change cassettes."
findings.fix: In ¶5 delete ", for example a rigid foam core within a washable outer skin," leaving "are of insulating construction". In ¶13 delete ", for example of moulded polymer," leaving "The rigid spacer frame 42 is a self-supporting rigid frame body".

findings.title: Undisclosed wick and pull-tab geometry (strip sized to the channel, tab as an end extension standing above the rim)
findings.detail: The inventor discloses that a removable absorbent wick lies in the shallow condensate channel and that a pull tab on the wick remains accessible when the tray is removed. Nothing states that the wick is a strip, that it is sized to the length of the channel, that the tab is an extension of that strip at one end, or that the tab stands above the channel rim. The figure brief then makes that same geometry the depicted structure, so the drawing would be the only source for it.
findings.evidence: disclosure.md: "A removable absorbent wick lies in a shallow condensate channel around the product tray... A pull tab on the wick remains accessible when the product tray is removed" — ¶43: "In some embodiments the removable absorbent wick 72 is a strip of absorbent material sized to the length of the shallow condensate channel 70, and the pull tab 74 is an extension of that strip at one end that stands above the rim of the shallow condensate channel 70."; figures/fig-04.md: "Pull tab 74: a short narrow tongue continuous with the inboard end of the wick 72, rising out of the channel 70 above the rim of the trough and clear of the wall 24."
findings.fix: Delete the last sentence of ¶43. In fig-04.md, reduce the two entries to the disclosed relationship: "Removable absorbent wick 72: an elongate body lying in the trough of the channel 70" and "Pull tab 74: a tab on the wick 72, drawn so that it is reachable from above when the tray is removed", deleting "occupying most of the width of the trough and standing lower than its rim" and "rising out of the channel 70 above the rim of the trough and clear of the wall 24".

findings.title: Claim 4 recites ledge and resilient-foot specifics that the disclosure does not give
findings.detail: The disclosure says the closing movement "presses resilient feet of the spacer frame against ledges of the shell so that the module cannot lift away from the tray during transport" and nothing more. That the ledges project inward from the shell side walls, that they sit at the level at which the module is seated, that the feet are compliant limbs of the frame, that they remain loaded while the carrier is closed and relax when the lid is opened, and that the module then lifts out by hand without a tool, are all candidate additions, and the first four are claimed.
findings.evidence: ¶35: "The ledges 18 project inward from the shell side walls 14 at the level at which the removable thermal module 40 is seated. The resilient feet 54 are compliant limbs of the rigid spacer frame 42, and the closing insulated lid 60 deflects them against the ledges 18 so that they remain loaded while the carrier is closed... When the insulated lid 60 is opened, the resilient feet 54 relax and the removable thermal module 40 lifts out by hand without a tool."; claim 4: "wherein the ledges project inward from the shell side walls at a level at which the removable thermal module is seated, and the resilient feet are compliant limbs of the rigid spacer frame that remain loaded against the ledges while the carrier is closed and relax when the insulated lid is opened."
findings.fix: Cancel claim 4 and renumber. In ¶35 keep the first sentence (which tracks the disclosure verbatim) and the sentence about the load holding the module down, and delete "The ledges 18 project inward from the shell side walls 14 at the level at which the removable thermal module 40 is seated. The resilient feet 54 are compliant limbs of the rigid spacer frame 42, and the closing insulated lid 60 deflects them against the ledges 18 so that they remain loaded while the carrier is closed." and the final sentence about relaxing and lifting out without a tool. findings.title: Tray feet "spaced apart" and a return passage "continuous from one side to the other" are added relationships
findings.detail: The disclosure states only that the tray is "suspended above the shell floor by feet so that a lower return passage remains under the tray". The candidate adds a spacing relationship between the feet and a continuity requirement for the return passage across the full width of the shell, claims it, and builds the FIG. 2 geometry on it. The continuity assertion is a functional flow relationship, not merely the inherent gap implied by plural feet.
findings.evidence: ¶7: "The tray feet 22 are spaced apart from one another so that the lower return passage 28 is continuous beneath the removable product tray 20 from one side of the insulated outer shell 10 to the other."; claim 7: "wherein the tray feet are spaced apart from one another so that the lower return passage is continuous beneath the removable product tray from one side of the insulated outer shell to the other"; figures/fig-02.md: "Short hatched supports stand between the bottom panel and the shell floor 12, spaced apart along the width so that the space between them runs continuously from left to right."
findings.fix: Delete that sentence from ¶7 and cancel claim 7 (whose remaining half is addressed by the perforation fix), renumbering. In fig-02.md replace the quoted sentence with "Short hatched supports stand between the bottom panel and the shell floor 12." and, in the Lower return passage 28 entry, delete "continuous from left to right between the short supports".

findings.title: Claim 14 recites a structural separation of the indicator interior from the circulation path that the disclosure does not state
findings.detail: The inventor's statement is functional and one sentence long: "The indicator does not control airflow." The candidate converts that into a structural limitation — that the indicator has an interior and that this interior is separate from the circulation path — and also asserts it in the description and in the FIG. 5 brief. The invariance of the circulation path between the retained and exposed states follows from the disclosed sentence; the structural separation of interiors does not.
findings.evidence: disclosure.md: "The indicator does not control airflow." — claim 14: "wherein the mechanical exposure indicator does not control airflow, an interior of the mechanical exposure indicator being separate from the circulation path and the circulation path being the same whether the indicator stem is retained by the temperature-responsive latch or has moved to the latched exposed position."; ¶51: "The interior of the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is separate from the circulation path"; figures/fig-05.md: "The interior of the indicator 80 is separate from the interior of the carrier and does not open into any internal passage of the carrier."
findings.fix: In claim 14 delete "an interior of the mechanical exposure indicator being separate from the circulation path and", leaving the functional recitation plus the path-invariance clause. Delete the sentence "The interior of the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is separate from the circulation path" from ¶51 and the corresponding Relationships bullet from fig-05.md.

findings.title: Assertion that no face of the payload contacts a cassette
findings.detail: The disclosure places the spacer frame above the tray and below the lid and says the cassettes are opposed, but never states that the payload is out of contact with a cassette, nor that the payload is conditioned by air rather than by conduction. The background separately identifies direct contact as a problem of prior containers, which makes this sentence read as an advantage assertion rather than a disclosed fact. I am less certain here than on the other fidelity items, because non-contact is close to a consequence of the frame resting above the tray; it is flagged as minor for that reason.
findings.evidence: ¶17: "and no face of the payload is in contact with a phase-change cassette 44. The payload is conditioned by the air that has passed the phase-change cassettes 44, rather than by conduction into a cassette lying on top of it." Disclosure: "The spacer frame rests above the product tray and below the lid."
findings.fix: Delete "and no face of the payload is in contact with a phase-change cassette 44" and the following sentence, leaving the disclosed observation that air entering between the opposed cassettes is exposed to two cooled faces at once.

findings.title: FIG. 5 geometry places a cassette against the shell wall, which conflicts with the module geometry of FIG. 3
findings.detail: FIG. 3 and the description put each cassette inside the spacer frame with a downward guide duct and an outboard frame web between the cassette's outboard surface and the shell side wall. FIG. 5 instead shows a cassette standing close to the shell's inner surface with the stem touching both, leaving no room for the duct or the outboard web. The description itself is neutral — it says only that the stem is "thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette 44" — so the conflict is between the two figure briefs, and it will be baked into the rendered sheets. Reported as minor because FIG. 5 is expressly a schematic wall-region section.
findings.evidence: figures/fig-05.md: "Phase-change cassette 44: a slab-like body inside the carrier at the right of the view... standing close to the inner surface of the shell 10 with the inner end of the stem 82 between them and touching both." versus figures/fig-03.md: "Downward guide duct 48: two blank open upright passages, one on each side, each between the outboard surface of one cassette 44 and the nearer outboard web of the frame 42", and ¶15: "Each downward guide duct 48 extends downward beside one of the phase-change cassettes 44".

findings.detail: Four of the five figures are sectional views, and FIG. 3 and FIG. 4 are enlargements of regions of the carrier, yet no brief places a broken cutting-plane line with a matching designation at each end and arrows in the viewing direction on any view, and the Brief Description never states which view a section is taken on.
